title: Fog
description: Looking straight up between the Canary Wharf towers into a summer cumulus sky, with air that knows how far away everything is. Drag up or scroll to shorten the visibility, down to clear it; the haze gathers a little thicker wherever the pointer rests. The far towers go first, turning the blue of the sky they stand in, the cumulus fade behind the veil while their edges stay crisp, and the glass corner overhead stays sharp in front of it all.
intent: Aerial perspective, after Makoto Shinkai's skyward city shots and the worm's-eye summer photographs herb loves: converging towers, a cobalt zenith, cumulus. Beer-Lambert transmittance per pixel and per channel (Rayleigh-leaning, blue extinguished first) through a haze layer that thins with height, along a metric distance converted from a Depth Anything V2 map. Drag sets the meteorological visibility (Koschmieder, beta = 3.912 / V) from 50 km to 150 m, mapped so the visible change runs evenly along the gesture: log V spends the clear-day kilometres, which change nothing in a 400 m frame, in the first tenth of the drag, so the far tower is already turning by fog 0.1 (~2 km), past half blue by 0.2 (~1.1 km), four fifths blue by 0.35 (~600 m) and a cobalt silhouette with the low sky veiled by 0.5 (~330 m). The extinction is depth-separated: the street around the viewer is swept clearer, the haze's density rising from nothing at the eye to full beyond about 60 m (a ray to d crosses d - d0 ln(1 + d / d0) of it), so the glass corner 30 m off sees a fifth of its straight-line air and keeps its contrast (within about 10% of a clear day at fog 0.5) while the far towers go. That clear pocket closes over the second half of the drag, which is what takes the near towers and the street. The in-scattered light comes from the sky itself. In front of a tower it is the open sky at that tower's own elevation, measured off the plate between the clouds (#5a9fcc low, deepening toward #2f7fb8), with extinction per channel and no lift toward white, so a far tower fades to a cyan-cobalt silhouette, never to milk, and it keeps its floor lines: the plate's local detail (the plate less a blur of the tower's own pixels at the scale of its floors) comes back over the in-scatter at the square root of the transmittance, never under about a third, so a fogged tower is a sky-tinted version of itself, faint cobalt on cobalt, not a flat slab. The haze is one medium along every line of sight, the sky and its cumulus included: a ray to a tower crosses the air out to that tower's distance, a ray past them crosses the haze column by airmass (1 / sin of its elevation, floored at 0.15) times the haze's density, and both take on the same in-scattered light at their elevation. Low down the street that light is the pale grey-blue of horizon haze (#A9C3D6), so the low sky and the gaps between the low cumulus lift and lose their saturation toward it (about s 0.45 at fog 0.55, where the clear plate is an electric s 0.86), easing higher up into the sky's own light, so the zenith stays deep cobalt and the sky deepens toward it. In front of a tower that light is a little dimmer (the canyon's air sees less of the sky), so a tower the haze has taken sits just under the sky behind it, never a lighter slab: its air light is held under 0.8 of the hazed sky or cloud luminance beside its silhouette, cloud shadow included. The air is also lit by the sun, which haze scatters forward: a Henyey-Greenstein lobe (g 0.6) toward the capture's sun, just past the top edge of the frame, warm-white (#FFF1E2) over the cumulus and in the sky's own colour over the open blue (warm-white over cobalt reads lilac), weighted by the air's opacity, so the clouds toward the sun stay cream under the haze while the low sky down the street, looking away from it, keeps its cyan. The air's light is held off the deepest shadows of anything still clearly seen, so the near glass keeps its black point while a far tower still fades whole. Distance and sky matte are snapped to the silhouettes (Depth Anything pulls a tower's edge toward the sky's distance for tens of pixels; each edge band takes its tower's interior distance instead), so the haze stops exactly where each tower does; the matte the air reads is coverage, not a switch: along each silhouette a guided filter on the plate's own colour softens the snapped matte onto the plate's edge, and every edge pixel blends the tower's distance and air with the sky's by how much of it is sky, so the silhouettes keep their sub-pixel shape at any size instead of stair-stepping. The far tower's roofline, where a reflection in the crown and the railing posts had bitten the matte, is closed and rebuilt with the same guided filter, so its top edge is clean. The haze in front of the sky only veils it, keeping at least 65% of the cumulus' local detail (the plate less its blur at the scale of the cloud's forms) so the low cloud reads as cloud through the air: forward-scatter softening touches the towers, never the clouds. The plate is two Poly Haven HDRIs (CC0, from their 16k captures) rendered at 3840 through the same stereographic rays: canary_wharf for the towers, docklands_01 for the sky, its cumulus unmixed from the capture's own blue, laid back over a radial cobalt (pale #2081AC where the sky meets the towers, #044984 in the middle of the opening) by a feathered cover so the edges thin as they did in the photograph, and split-graded from cyan-grey (#B7C5C5) in the shaded folds through #DFE1DE to #FFF1E2 on the sunlit tops; the same split grade runs again after the haze, on the luminance the haze left and weighted by how much of a pixel's light is the sun's, so a veiled cumulus top still lands on the warm end instead of the air's cyan. A film finish runs last: a diffusion bloom, a filmic shoulder whose top is warm (above about 0.9 in luminance the light rolls off toward cream #FFF1E2, never neutral paper-white), glass graded away from the sky's blue, a thin amber halation under the highlight edges (the sunlit cumulus and glints only, never the pale cyan sky against a tower), and 24 fps grain at scan scale held for two frames.
